subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A medical student auscultates a healthy 25-year-old man. She hears a sound at the beginning of systole that is loudest at the mitral area (apex) and coincides with the upstroke of the arterial pulse.
question: Which of the following best explains the origin of this sound?

options.text: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Turbulence during rapid ventricular filling in early diastole
Atrial contraction propelling blood into a stiffened ventricle in late diastole
Turbulence from blood flowing across an open, narrowed valve
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves

explanation_correct: The sound described is S1, produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of ventricular systole. It is loudest at the mitral area and coincides with the onset of the arterial pulse.

explanation_incorrect.A: Aortic and pulmonary valve closure produces S2, which occurs at the end of systole and is loudest at the left upper sternal border.
explanation_incorrect.B: Rapid ventricular filling in early diastole can produce S3, a low-pitched sound after S2, not a sound at the onset of systole.
explanation_incorrect.C: Atrial contraction into a stiffened ventricle in late diastole produces S4, which occurs just before S1, not at the pulse upstroke.
explanation_incorrect.D: Turbulence across an open narrowed valve produces a murmur, not the discrete first heart sound heard at the onset of systole.

educationalObjective: S1 is produced by mitral and tricuspid valve closure and is loudest at the mitral (apical) area.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 58-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and biventricular heart failure is evaluated for worsening dyspnea. With the patient in the left lateral decubitus position, a low-pitched sound is heard at the apex in early diastole, immediately after S2. An echocardiogram shows a dilated left ventricle with an increased end-systolic volume.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this finding?

options.text: Atrial contraction against a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle in late diastole
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the onset of systole
Turbulence during rapid ventricular filling, caused by blood from the left atrium mixing with an increased end-systolic volume
Regurgitant flow across the aortic valve throughout diastole
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves in late diastole

explanation_correct: The sound is an S3, heard in early diastole during the rapid ventricular filling phase. It is associated with increased filling pressures (eg, mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, heart failure, thyrotoxicosis) and is more common in dilated ventricles; the turbulence is caused by blood from the left atrium mixing with the increased end-systolic volume. It is best heard at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position.

explanation_incorrect.A: Atrial contraction into a stiff, hypertrophied ventricle in late diastole produces S4, which occurs just before S1, not early diastole after S2.
explanation_incorrect.B: Mitral and tricuspid valve closure produces S1, a sharp systolic sound, not a low-pitched early diastolic sound after S2.
explanation_incorrect.D: Aortic regurgitation is a diastolic decrescendo murmur that can raise filling pressures and contribute to an S3, but the S3 itself is generated by rapid filling turbulence, not by the regurgitant jet.
explanation_incorrect.E: Aortic and pulmonary valve closure produces S2, which occurs at the end of systole; the patient's finding follows S2 in early diastole.

educationalObjective: S3 occurs in early diastole during rapid ventricular filling; it reflects increased filling pressures and dilated ventricles, with turbulence from left atrial blood mixing with increased end-systolic volume.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 72-year-old woman with longstanding hypertension and echocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy is auscultated. A low-pitched sound is heard at the apex in late diastole, immediately before S1, with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position. Her heart rhythm is regular, and an S1 is clearly audible.
question: Which mechanism best explains this finding?

options.text: Atrial contraction (the 'atrial kick') propelling blood into a stiff, noncompliant left ventricle
Turbulence from rapid filling of a dilated left ventricle in early diastole
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of ventricular systole
Regurgitant flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole

explanation_correct: The sound is an S4, heard in late diastole (the 'atrial kick') when atrial contraction drives blood into a stiffened, noncompliant ventricle, as in hypertrophy. It is associated with ventricular noncompliance and high atrial pressure, is best heard at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position, is considered abnormal if palpable, and is common in older adults.

explanation_incorrect.B: Rapid filling of a dilated ventricle in early diastole produces S3, which occurs just after S2, not immediately before S1.
explanation_incorrect.C: Mitral and tricuspid closure produces S1; the sound here precedes S1 and therefore occurs in late diastole.
explanation_incorrect.D: Aortic and pulmonary closure produces S2, which marks the end of systole; the finding described occurs in late diastole, long after S2.
explanation_incorrect.E: Mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic murmur that can raise filling pressures and predispose to an S3, but a discrete late diastolic sound before S1 is generated by atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle.

educationalObjective: S4 is a late diastolic sound ('atrial kick') produced by blood entering a stiffened, noncompliant ventricle, typically from hypertrophy.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 68-year-old man with chronic atrial fibrillation is evaluated. His pulse is irregularly irregular, his electrocardiogram shows no organized atrial activity, and his jugular venous pulsations lack distinct presystolic waves.
question: Which heart sound would be expected to be absent in this patient?

options.text: S1
S2
S3
S4
Both S1 and S2

explanation_correct: S4 is generated by atrial contraction (the 'atrial kick') in late diastole, forcing blood into a stiffened ventricle. In atrial fibrillation there is no coordinated atrial contraction, which is also why the a wave of the jugular venous pulse is absent, so an S4 cannot be generated.

explanation_incorrect.A: S1 is produced by mitral and tricuspid valve closure at the onset of systole and does not require atrial contraction, so it remains present.
explanation_incorrect.B: S2 is produced by aortic and pulmonary valve closure at the end of systole and does not require atrial contraction, so it remains present.
explanation_incorrect.C: S3 is produced during rapid ventricular filling in early diastole and can occur without atrial contraction, so it is not necessarily absent.
explanation_incorrect.E: S1 and S2 both result from valve closure during each cardiac cycle and continue to be present in atrial fibrillation.

educationalObjective: S4 requires coordinated atrial contraction (atrial kick) and therefore cannot be present in atrial fibrillation, just as the JVP a wave is absent.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: During a routine physical examination, a student hears the second heart sound (S2) and asks where it is normally heard loudest and what produces it.
question: Which response is correct?

options.text: S2 is produced by mitral and tricuspid valve closure and is loudest at the apex
S2 is produced by atrial contraction and is loudest at the right upper sternal border
S2 is produced by mitral valve closure alone and is loudest at the left lower sternal border
S2 is produced by aortic and pulmonary valve closure and is loudest at the left upper sternal border
S2 is produced by rapid ventricular filling and is loudest over the epigastrium

explanation_correct: S2 is produced by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of ventricular systole and is loudest at the left upper sternal border, in contrast to S1, which is loudest at the mitral area.

explanation_incorrect.A: Mitral and tricuspid valve closure produces S1, not S2, and it is loudest at the mitral (apical) area.
explanation_incorrect.B: Atrial contraction produces S4 in late diastole, not the second heart sound, and S4 is best heard at the apex, not the right upper sternal border.
explanation_incorrect.C: S2 involves both the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, not the mitral valve alone, and it is loudest at the left upper sternal border.
explanation_incorrect.E: Rapid ventricular filling produces S3 in early diastole, which is best heard at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position, not over the epigastrium.

educationalObjective: S2 is produced by aortic and pulmonary valve closure and is loudest at the left upper sternal border.
